title: The Hardest Games for AI May Be the Smallest
author: ia-bin
selftext:
I’ve been using AI pretty heavily for game development lately, and I’ve started to think the phrase “game development has no barrier anymore” is only half true.

AI is getting ridiculously good at building things that already have well-known patterns.

Platformers, shooters, RPG systems, 3D environments, dialogue, assets, animations, UI — there are tons of existing examples for AI to learn from. And generative AI is also rapidly cutting the cost of 3D asset production, which used to be a huge barrier for solo developers and small teams.

But I’ve had almost the opposite experience with small puzzle games.

If the mechanic is genuinely new, AI suddenly has much less to copy.

The hard part isn’t drawing the UI or writing Swift/Kotlin/C++ anymore. It’s things like:

How do you randomly generate effectively unlimited levels?

How do you guarantee every generated state is solvable?

How do you avoid “technically valid” levels that are strategically doomed?

How do you generate them fast enough that players don’t think the game froze?

I ran into this repeatedly while developing my own Playable Image games.

With iaReveal, if I didn’t describe the chain-reaction initialization logic precisely enough, AI naturally drifted toward something much closer to a normal puzzle/jigsaw implementation.

With iaBrick, random generation could work perfectly from a coding perspective, but without explicit solvability constraints some boards could become effectively unwinnable.

With iaStroke, the generated boards could be valid, but a naïve search algorithm could take far too long to initialize a new game.

That’s when I realized something:

AI is removing the implementation barrier much faster than it is removing the invention barrier.

If a mechanic already exists, AI can often reproduce it amazingly well.

But if the mechanic is new, somebody still has to define the state space, constraints, invariants, solvability conditions, search strategy, and optimization approach.

And that part can be much harder than writing the code.

So weirdly, I’m starting to think some tiny original puzzle games may be harder for AI to build well than visually spectacular games based on familiar mechanics.

Not because they need more code.

Because there’s less existing knowledge to copy.

That’s been one of the most interesting lessons for me while building Playable Image / iaReveal with AI.

Curious if other game devs using AI have run into the same thing.

comments.author: Novaworld7
comments.body:
I'm not going to read all of that.

Though this new found land concept you refer to is only restricted by your knowledge on the subject and our the knowledge you have with regards to your own development.

I.e. if you've not built a proper GDD or TDD then anything you eventually build will end up going in cycles of "oh shiny object", and "nuke and start over." 

Once you know what you are trying to build, the limitation becomes your knowledge and or your ability to explain what you want, not AI's inability to produce. 

Most if not all barrier to software has been erroded significantly.

replies.author: PetiteGousseDAil
replies.body:
100% this.

When you know swe, you know how to build a code base that limits the complexity hell curve. TDD and Clean Code are the way to go.

replies.author: ia-bin
replies.body:
I think we're actually pretty close on this.

Once the design is well specified, I agree that the limitation becomes my own knowledge and how precisely I can communicate it. AI is usually very good at implementation at that point.

Where I've found it harder is that, with a new mechanic, I don't always know the full specification at the beginning. Some of the important constraints only become obvious after prototyping and finding failure cases.

A GDD can say “generated boards must always be solvable,” but that still doesn't tell you *how* to construct them, how to verify that efficiently, whether technically solvable states are actually fair, or what tradeoffs you're willing to make.

So I don't really see that as AI failing to follow a finished plan. The interesting part to me is that creating the plan itself can be a large part of the technical work.

replies.author: Novaworld7
replies.body:
That's not AI failing though. That's you failing. I wouldn't put your failure on the AI. 

You should poke and prod/ brainstorm with AI before attempting to implement before saying something like, paint the wall red ... No, not that red, another red. 

Edit: 

On your board example, that's not a good GDD by the way. That's an idea / concept. You are failing to describe what the board is, how users interact with the board, what the point of the board is etc there should be many more points to that concept that make it build able. Failure to do so means that the AI is left to interpret, and when that happens your mileage may vary. 

Secondly yes, the burden has shifted from building to describing. That's not new. Also QA. You are not in QA land where you will spend 100x more time than building.

comments.author: PetiteGousseDAil
comments.body:
Not really. Complex puzzle games do need more code than a simple open world RPG.

Bigger environment doesn't mean more code.

And AI if far past the "there are no solutions online so it's not good with that". You're just encountering the wall in swe where complexity increases exponentially with the size of your code base.

Making a game where you run around and hit enemies with a sword is not complex. It's not a lot of code. It's not hard to maintain.

Puzzle games have tons of constraints and logic. These add complexity.

It's not about the size in terms of visually impressive or big environment, it's the size of the code base that makes AI less efficient.

replies.author: ia-bin
replies.body:
That's a good distinction, and I think “small” was probably too imprecise in my wording.

I meant small in presentation and asset scope, not necessarily small in logical complexity or code.

A puzzle game can look extremely simple while having a dense set of interacting constraints, state transitions, search problems, and edge cases. A visually large game can have much more content and production work while still relying on relatively familiar systems.

So I agree that part of what I'm seeing may simply be software complexity rather than “AI has never seen this before.”

Where I still think novelty matters is that, when the mechanic is unusual, I'm also spending more time discovering what the constraints should even be, rather than just managing an already-understood complex system.

I probably should have framed the distinction more as “visual/production complexity vs constraint/logic complexity” rather than big game vs small game.

comments.author: dorcsyful
comments.body: So what you're saying is that if you don't tell the AI what exactly to do it starts to attempt to fill the holes by itself?

replies.author: ia-bin
replies.body:
Pretty much, yes — but the important part for me is *how* it fills those holes.

If the mechanic is familiar, those guesses are often useful because there are established patterns to fall back on.

If the mechanic is unusual, the AI still has to make assumptions, and those assumptions can quietly pull the implementation toward something more conventional than what I actually intended.

So the issue isn't just that it fills in missing details. It's that with a new mechanic, the default assumptions themselves can be wrong.

replies.author: dorcsyful
replies.body:
AI is, by definition unable to come up with original things, so you really should not be surprised that it goes for what you call "normal puzzle".
I'm not sure what kind of game you're making and how it's going wrong but there are a million different ways for creating unique levels/puzzles. If you don't give it either the exact algorithm(s) to implement or plenty of examples to derive data from it's going to choose one at random and produce what you call incorrect.
